view: This is the third commercial quarter of YARTEMLEA, the only approved TA-TMA drug, and the stock trades on whether the ramp continued after a near-tripling in Q2 ($9.9M to $28.5M net; ordering accounts up from 30 to 73; distributor inventory steady at about 1.5 weeks, so no stocking). My own arithmetic: Q2 averaged roughly 50 ordering accounts (30 at the start, 73 at the end) at about $0.55M per account per quarter. Q3 starts with at least 73 accounts, a full quarter of the permanent J-code (from 1 July) and formulary approval at 55-60% of the top centres. That puts Q3 net revenue around $36-45M even if per-account productivity falls as smaller centres come on. The one dated trace from after quarter-end points the same way. On 2026-10-16, with Q3 in hand, management ended EU compassionate use, citing 'increasing demand for YARTEMLEA drug supply in the U.S. commercial market' and 'rapid U.S. commercial adoption'. A company that knew Q3 had stalled would be unlikely to write that. A weaker trace: on 10-28 the board granted the CEO a 500k performance option struck at the $17.88 close, after the quarter closed and before the print. Against that, the higher consensus ($37-38M) already assumes a +31% step. Q2's jump may partly have been pent-up demand. Per-patient demand at a centre is episodic, so 'cumulative accounts' overstates active use. And the options already price a 16-17% move, with the upside side the more expensive. My distribution: a clear beat of $38M+ (about 55-60%) probably lifts a 17%-of-float short book sharply; $33-38M is a split read against the conflicting consensus figures; below $33M would confirm the 'pent-up demand' bear case and fall hard. Overall a modest tilt up, not enough to bet.
unpriced: Possibly some of the ramp. Sell-side 3-year numbers (about $298M revenue in 2029, per a Simply Wall St summary) and a $30.9M print consensus sit below Q2's exit run-rate, and the 10-16 'increasing U.S. demand' statement was buried under the EU headline that took the stock down 14% that day. Coverage is thin (about 3-4 analysts) and the consensus figures disagree by $7M, so a $40M print could read as a large beat on several screens. The higher consensus and the call skew show that much of this is known, so the gap is small.

recommendation.reason: The inputs to the revenue line point up: account count and reimbursement arithmetic, and the company's own post-quarter 'increasing demand' wording. A crowded short makes a beat move more. But the better-informed consensus already asks for +31% sequentially, the call skew shows the upside is partly bought, and no independent demand series (scripts, claims, channel checks) was found to show Q3 clears $38M. Below the 65 bar, so no position.
recommendation.what_would_flip_it: Q3 net revenue at or below about $33M, or a flat ordering-account count / falling reorder frequency, which would confirm that Q2 was pent-up demand.

self_critique: The best-informed consensus ($37-38M) already asks for a +31% step, and the call skew shows buyers are paying for the upside. A $36-38M print could be read as in line, or as a slowdown from Q2's tripling, and launch stocks often sell off on that. Q2 may have held pent-up patients (Q1 was a mid-January partial launch), making Q3 the first clean read. And 'increasing demand' language from a CEO in a dispute with the EMA is advocacy, not data. Under this view the true p_up is near 50, which is why I stay at 60 and do not recommend.
approach_notes: P4 and P7 helped: rebuilding the revenue line from accounts, and treating the conflicting consensus figures as unproven priced-in claims. P3's worker/customer/physical sources had nothing to reach for an in-hospital orphan drug with thin coverage, so the view rests on company statements and arithmetic.
